claim: Communication in neural circuits across the cortex is thought to be mediated by spontaneous temporally organized patterns of population activity lasting ~50-200 ms.
source: Communication in neural circuits across the cortex is thought to be mediated by spontaneous temporally organized patterns of population activity lasting ~50 –200 ms.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural communication that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Current brain-computer interfaces are not designed to interpret multi-neuronal spiking patterns at the millisecond timescale.
source: Current brain–computer interfaces, however, are not designed to interpret multi-neuronal spiking patterns at the millisecond timescale.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current technology that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: The developed system decodes multi-neuronal patterns at 10 ms resolution.
source: Our system decodes multi-neuronal patterns at 10 ms resolution, identifies within 50 ms experience-related patterns with over 70% sensitivity and specificity, and classifies their content with 95% accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing the system's temporal resolution.

claim: The system identifies experience-related patterns within 50 ms with over 70% sensitivity and specificity.
source: Our system decodes multi-neuronal patterns at 10 ms resolution, identifies within 50 ms experience-related patterns with over 70% sensitivity and specificity, and classifies their content with 95% accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance metrics calculated from experimental data.

claim: The system classifies replay content with 95% accuracy.
source: Our system decodes multi-neuronal patterns at 10 ms resolution, identifies within 50 ms experience-related patterns with over 70% sensitivity and specificity, and classifies their content with 95% accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by accuracy measurements from experimental testing.

claim: Brief multi-neuronal spiking sequences lasting 50-200 ms have been revealed in cortical networks by large-scale recordings.
source: Large-scale recordings have revealed the presence of brief (50–200 ms) multi-neuronal spiking sequences in cortical networks.
evidence: This statement references findings from prior research in the field.

claim: Brief sequences appear as rapid increases in multi-unit firing rate and are generated endogenously or in response to external stimulus.
source: The brief sequences appear as rapid increases in the multi-unit firing rate and they are generated endogenously or in response to an external stimulus (Luczak et al., 2009Luczak et al., 2007; Luczak et al., 2009; Pasquale et al., 2017; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Riehle et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The omnipresence of these activity patterns in the cortical mantle suggests they constitute the basic elements of the cortical neural code.
source: The omnipresence of these activity patterns in the cortical mantle suggests that they constitute the basic elements of the cortical neural code (Harris, 2005; Luczak, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Large-scale recordings in rodents revealed the occurrence of accelerated 'replays' of spatial information during sleeping and resting states.
source: In rodents, large-scale recordings revealed the occurrence of accelerated 'replays' of the spatial information encoded in the population activity during an experience (e.g. traversal of an arm in a maze), both during sleeping and when in a resting state (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Structured firing of experience-related activity was reported in entorhinal, neocortical, and subcortical circuits.
source: Structured firing of experience-related activity was also reported in entorhinal (O'Neill et al., 2017; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2016), neocortical (Hoffman and McNaughton, 2002; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Peyrache et al., 2009; Qin et al., 1997; Ribeiro et al., 2004; Rothschild et al., 2017) and subcortical (Girardeau et al., 2017; Gomperts et al., 2015; Lansink et al., 2008; Pennartz et al., 2004; Valdés et al., 2015) circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research across different brain regions.

claim: Distinct replay sequences might be used for sharing information with the neocortex for system-level memory consolidation.
source: Correlative analyses of the multi-neuronal spike content of hippocampal replay suggest that distinct replay sequences might be used for sharing information with the neocortex, specifically for system-level memory consolidation (Axmacher et al., 2009; Dupret et al., 2010; Lewis and Durrant, 2011)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by correlative analyses cited from prior research.

claim: Replay sequences might be used for creation and update of an internal model for covert evaluation of possible outcomes during memory-guided decision-making.
source: and for the creation and update of an internal model for covert evaluation of possible outcomes during memory-guided decision-making (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2017; Penny et al., 2013; Pezzulo et al., 2014; Pezzulo et al., 2017;Pezzulo et al., 2014; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013;Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Closed-loop manipulations of replay-related activity are limited to real-time detection of fast sharp-wave ripple oscillations (120-250 Hz).
source: Closed-loop manipulations of replay-related activity are to date limited to the use of real-time detection of fast sharp-wave ripple (SWR) oscillations (120 – 250 Hz) (Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Girardeau et al., 2009; Girardeau et al., 2014; Jadhav et al., 2012; Kovács et al., 2016; Maingret et al., 2016;Nokia et al., 2010; Nokia et al., 2012; Novitskaya et al., 2016; Roux et al., 2017; Talakoub et al., 2016; van de Ven et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior closed-loop studies.

claim: Sharp-wave ripple oscillations reflect merely the bursting state of the neuronal population but not the actual replay content.
source: that reflect merely the bursting state of the neuronal population but not the actual replay content.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the limitations of prior methods based on understanding of SWR physiology.

claim: Any causal link between replay content and behavior or physiology remains untested.
source: Any causal link between replay content and behavior or physiology thus remains untested.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge based on the limitations of prior methods.

claim: A closed-loop manipulation is necessary to provide a direct causal link between a specific transient neural activity pattern and its hypothesized contribution to cognition.
source: To provide a direct causal link between a specific transient neural activity pattern and its hypothesized contribution to cognition, correlational and computational studies are not sufficient and a closed-loop manipulation is necessary (Hady, 2016; Potter et al., 2014; Zrenner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological principle supported by citations to prior work on experimental design.

claim: A complete methodology for detecting re-expressed spike patterns within tens of milliseconds has not yet been demonstrated.
source: but a complete methodology for detecting (re)expressed spike patterns within tens of milliseconds has not yet been demonstrated.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current technology that the manuscript addresses.

claim: Offline identification algorithms generally require all data to be available or are not suitable for an online scenario.
source: The rapid detection of multi-neuronal patterns in a closed-loop setting is challenging because offline identification algorithms generally require all data to be available or are otherwise not suitable for an online scenario.
evidence: This is a technical observation about the limitations of offline algorithms.

claim: Offline algorithms often have intensive computational demands that pose challenges for real-time execution at tens of millisecond latency.
source: Moreover, the algorithms often have intensive computational demands that pose challenges for real-time execution at tens of millisecond latency.
evidence: This is a technical observation about computational constraints.

claim: Brain-computer interfaces for motor control generally operate sufficiently with latencies of 120-200 ms.
source: Such requirements are not present in brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) and other neuroprostheses for motor control as they generally operate sufficiently with latencies of 120 – 200 ms (Ibáñez et al., 2014; Velliste et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior BCI research.

claim: Motor control BCI latencies are one order of magnitude greater than required for rapid detection of transient cortical multi-neuronal sequences.
source: one order of magnitude greater than is required for the rapid detection of transient cortical multi-neuronal sequences.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the temporal requirements of different neural phenomena.

claim: The system builds on previous work describing efficient offline implementation of spike-sorting-less neural decoding.
source: The system builds on our previous work describing an efficient offline implementation of spike-sorting-less neural decoding (Kloosterman et al., 2014; Sodkomkham et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors as the foundation for the current system.

claim: The system builds on a general software framework (Falcon) for complex online neural processing in closed-loop settings.
source: and a general software framework (Falcon) for complex online neural processing in closed-loop settings (Ciliberti and Kloosterman, 2017).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors as the foundation for the current system.

claim: The system performed real-time population decoding of spatial information from CA1 assemblies at 10 ms temporal resolution.
source: Using this novel closed-loop system, we performed real-time population decoding of spatial information from CA1 assemblies at the stringent 10 ms temporal resolution and detected distinct classes of replay at a low 50 ms average latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The system detected distinct classes of replay at a low 50 ms average latency.
source: Using this novel closed-loop system, we performed real-time population decoding of spatial information from CA1 assemblies at the stringent 10 ms temporal resolution and detected distinct classes of replay at a low 50 ms average latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements from experimental data.

claim: Real-time identification of population bursts with replay had more than 70% average sensitivity and specificity.
source: Real-time identification of population bursts with replay had more than 70% average sensitivity and specificity, whereas content classification accuracy was on average over 95%.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance metrics calculated from experimental data.

claim: Content classification accuracy was on average over 95%.
source: Real-time identification of population bursts with replay had more than 70% average sensitivity and specificity, whereas content classification accuracy was on average over 95%.
evidence: This claim is supported by accuracy measurements from experimental data.

claim: The technology was demonstrated in a freely behaving rat during both resting and awake states using in vivo large-scale recordings.
source: We demonstrated this technology in a freely behaving rat during both resting and awake states using in vivo large-scale recordings.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental conditions under which the system was tested.

claim: Detection algorithm parameters can be adjusted to trade off sensitivity and specificity or latency and accuracy.
source: We also illustrated that detection algorithm parameters can be adjusted, depending on the requirements of the experiment, to trade off sensitivity and specificity or latency and accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by parameter sweep analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Detection performance is affected by the number of recording channels.
source: We further showed how detection performance is affected by the number of recording channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses varying the number of tetrodes.

claim: The system addressed three general major technical challenges.
source: Our system addressed three general major technical challenges.
evidence: This introduces the technical challenges that the manuscript describes addressing.

claim: The determination of replay content should be completed with minimal data, which introduces a trade-off between algorithmic detection latency and detection accuracy.
source: The first challenge derives from the desire to respond to an identified replay as soon as possible after the event has started (and well before it is over). Thus, the determination of replay content should be completed with minimal data, which inevitably introduces a trade-off between algorithmic detection latency and detection accuracy.
evidence: This describes a fundamental constraint in the design of the system.

claim: The exact start and end times of replay events are unknown and cannot be predicted in an online scenario.
source: Second, any approach for online detection of hippocampal replay content must be suitable for data arriving as a continuous live stream; in such a scenario, the exact start (and end) times of replay events are unknown and cannot be predicted.
evidence: This describes a constraint of online processing.

claim: The constraints of the online scenario require the implementation to make use of past-observed information only.
source: The constraints of the online scenario require the implementation to make use of past-observed information only.
evidence: This describes a fundamental constraint of causal online processing.

claim: Real-time computations should only minimally increase the overall detection latency.
source: As a third challenge, the real-time computations needed to identify replay content in the continuous high-volume and high-rate stream should only minimally increase the overall detection latency, which should be dominated by its algorithmic contribution.
evidence: This describes a design goal for the computational implementation.

claim: The need for fast computations introduces a possible latency-accuracy trade-off where approximate algorithms may be required to meet real-time deadlines.
source: The need for fast computations introduces another possible latency–accuracy trade-off, in which approximate algorithms may be required to meet real-time deadlines.
evidence: This describes a potential trade-off in the system design.

claim: The system is built on top of the Falcon open source framework for closed-loop neuroscience.
source: Built on top of the Falcon open source framework for closed-loop neuroscience (Ciliberti and Kloosterman, 2017), the system reads and processes a continuous stream of multi-channel neural signals, analyzes the signals to search for potential replay events and emits a digital output pulse upon the detection of a replay event containing target content
evidence: This describes the software foundation of the system with citation to prior work.

claim: The system reads and processes a continuous stream of multi-channel neural signals.
source: the system reads and processes a continuous stream of multi-channel neural signals, analyzes the signals to search for potential replay events and emits a digital output pulse upon the detection of a replay event containing target content
evidence: This describes the basic functionality of the system.

claim: The system emits a digital output pulse upon detection of a replay event containing target content.
source: the system reads and processes a continuous stream of multi-channel neural signals, analyzes the signals to search for potential replay events and emits a digital output pulse upon the detection of a replay event containing target content
evidence: This describes the output behavior of the system.

claim: The target was defined as a replay trajectory of one of the tracks in a multi-arm maze.
source: We defined the target as a replay trajectory of one of the tracks in a multi-arm maze (e.g. a Y-maze).
evidence: This describes the experimental definition of target replay content.

claim: Neural population decoding followed by characterization of spatial-temporal structure in decoded locations was applied to detect replay content.
source: To detect replay content, we applied neural population decoding followed by the characterization of the spatial-temporal structure in the decoded locations (Figure 1b), similar to the approach that is often used for offline replay analysis (Davidson et al., 2009; Kloosterman, 2011).
evidence: This describes the algorithmic approach with citation to prior methods.

claim: The incoming data stream is continuously decoded in 10 ms bins.
source: The incoming data stream is continuously decoded in 10 ms bins and, on the basis of the most recent 30 ms of decoded spiking activity, an assessment is made of whether or not a population burst with replay of one of the maze arms is present.
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution of the decoding process.

claim: An assessment of replay presence is made based on the most recent 30 ms of decoded spiking activity.
source: The incoming data stream is continuously decoded in 10 ms bins and, on the basis of the most recent 30 ms of decoded spiking activity, an assessment is made of whether or not a population burst with replay of one of the maze arms is present.
evidence: This describes the integration window used for replay detection.

claim: Modest compression of the encoding model reduced computational costs, resulting in online decode time below 1 ms per spike.
source: Modest compression of the encoding model reduced the computational costs, resulting in an online decode time below 1 ms per spike, without affecting the system's ability to decode the animal's position during run epochs (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational timing measurements shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Compression of the encoding model did not affect the system's ability to decode the animal's position during run epochs.
source: Modest compression of the encoding model reduced the computational costs, resulting in an online decode time below 1 ms per spike, without affecting the system's ability to decode the animal's position during run epochs (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding accuracy analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The effect of compression on posterior probability distributions in candidate replay bursts is small for low to moderate compression levels.
source: The effect of compression on the integrity of posterior probability distributions in candidate replay population bursts is small for low to moderate compression levels, in particular for posteriors that have a MAP estimate with high probability (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The determination of replay content and triggering of digital output pulse occurred within 2.2 ms of data acquisition in over 95% of cases.
source: Overall, the implementation of the algorithms, including the spike-by-spike construction of posterior probability distributions and parallel processing (see 'Materials and methods'), made sure that the determination of replay content and the triggering of a corresponding digital output pulse occurred within 2.2 ms of the time at which the neural data were acquired in over 95% of the cases (Figure 1e; median added latency: 1.1 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The median added latency was 1.1 ms.
source: Overall, the implementation of the algorithms, including the spike-by-spike construction of posterior probability distributions and parallel processing (see 'Materials and methods'), made sure that the determination of replay content and the triggering of a corresponding digital output pulse occurred within 2.2 ms of the time at which the neural data were acquired in over 95% of the cases (Figure 1e; median added latency: 1.1 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Stress tests showed that added latency remains low for high per-tetrode spike rates and large number of tetrodes (up to 32) on a 32-core workstation.
source: Stress tests of the system with artificially generated spikes showed that the added latency remains low for high per-tetrode spike rates and for a large number of tetrodes (up to 32) on a 32-core workstation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), thus demonstrating the scalability of our solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by stress test results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Performance on a 4-core workstation is similar to 32-core workstation for up to 24 tetrodes and per-tetrode spike rates matching the datasets.
source: Additional tests on a 4-core workstation revealed that added latency has higher variability, especially in the case of 32 tetrodes and high spike rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), but that performance is similar to that of the 32-core workstation for up to 24 tetrodes and per-tetrode spike rates that match our datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative stress test results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hippocampal ensemble activity was recorded using tetrodes in a rat that repeatedly explored the arms of a 3-arm radial maze.
source: To test our closed-loop framework of online detection of replay content, we recorded hippocampal ensemble activity using tetrodes in a rat that repeatedly explored the arms of a 3-arm radial maze.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: A first exposure to the maze (RUN1) was used to prepare the encoding model for online neural decoding.
source: In each of the three separate recording sessions, a first exposure to the maze (RUN1) was used to prepare the encoding model for online neural decoding.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Cross-validation showed good decoding performance in RUN1 with a median error below 10 cm.
source: Cross-validation showed good decoding performance in RUN1 with a median error below 10 cm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a), which required only a few traversals of the maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Good decoding performance required only a few traversals of the maze.
source: Cross-validation showed good decoding performance in RUN1 with a median error below 10 cm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a), which required only a few traversals of the maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Real-time closed-loop replay content detection was activated in a subsequent rest epoch (REST) and in a second exposure to the radial maze (RUN2).
source: Real-time closed-loop replay content detection was activated in a subsequent rest epoch (REST) and in a second exposure to the radial maze (RUN2).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The encoding model built using data from RUN1 was valid for decoding the animal's position in RUN2.
source: The encoding model built using data from RUN1 was also valid for decoding the animal's position in RUN2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), indicating that recordings were stable and spatial representations had not remapped (Anderson and Jeffery, 2003; Latuske et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding performance analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Stable recordings and lack of remapping are indicated by the validity of the encoding model across RUN1 and RUN2.
source: The encoding model built using data from RUN1 was also valid for decoding the animal's position in RUN2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), indicating that recordings were stable and spatial representations had not remapped (Anderson and Jeffery, 2003; Latuske et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the decoding performance data, supported by citations to prior work on remapping.

claim: No actual feedback perturbation of brain activity was applied to evaluate online detection performance without distortions of the signal.
source: To evaluate the online detection performance without distortions of the signal, no actual feedback perturbation of brain activity was applied to the brain.
evidence: This describes an experimental design choice.

claim: Reference hippocampal population bursts were defined offline based on the detrended MUA signal.
source: Reference hippocampal population bursts were defined offline on the basis of the detrended MUA signal and classified as either associated or not associated with replay (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the method for creating a reference dataset for evaluation.

claim: The offline reference dataset contained a total of 3506 population bursts recorded in REST (n=1321) and RUN2 (n=2185) across all three sessions.
source: The offline reference data set contained a total of 3506 population bursts that were recorded in REST (n = 1321) and RUN2 (n = 2185) across all three sessions.
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics of the reference dataset.

claim: The median duration of reference bursts was 83.0 ms (inter-quartile range [65.3, 119.8]).
source: The median duration of reference bursts was 83.0 ms (inter-quartile range (iqr) [65.3, 119.8]; REST: median 89.0 ms, iqr [70.0, 126.0]; RUN2: median 79.0 ms, iqr [63.0, 116.0]).
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics of burst durations.

claim: In RUN2, the majority of reference bursts occurred when the animal paused at the distal reward platforms.
source: In RUN2, the majority of reference bursts occurred when the animal paused at the distal reward platforms.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data.

claim: Online closed-loop replay identification resulted in a total of 2123 positive hits.
source: Online, closed-loop replay identification resulted in a total of 2123 positive hits, a large majority of which (87.3%, 1854/2123) were associated with reference bursts.
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics of online detection results.

claim: 87.3% (1854/2123) of online positive hits were associated with reference bursts.
source: Online, closed-loop replay identification resulted in a total of 2123 positive hits, a large majority of which (87.3%, 1854/2123) were associated with reference bursts.
evidence: This provides a performance metric for the online detection system.

claim: Very few online detections occurred immediately before and within 20 ms after reference burst onset, or after burst offset.
source: Very few online detections occurred immediately before and within 20 ms after reference burst onset, or after burst offset (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the peri-event time histogram shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A small fraction of hits were non-burst false positives, predominantly in the third test session.
source: A small fraction of hits were non-burst false positives (FPnon_burst), predominantly in the third test session (Table 2).
evidence: This describes a category of detection errors with reference to data in Table 2.

claim: There was a slightly higher fraction of positive hits inside reference bursts in REST (91.9%, 694/755) compared to RUN2 (84.8%, 1160/1368).
source: There was a slightly higher fraction of positive hits inside reference bursts in REST (91.9%, 694/755) as compared to RUN2 (84.8%, 1160/1368).
evidence: This provides a comparison of detection performance between behavioral states.

claim: 80.6% of non-burst false positives in RUN2 occurred when the rat was moving (speed > 5 cm/s).
source: Indeed, 80.6% of FPnon_burst in RUN2 occurred when the rat was moving (speed > 5 cm/s), whereas the majority of online detections inside reference bursts (73.8%) occurred when the rat was immobile (speed < 5 cm/s).
evidence: This provides behavioral context for false positive detections.

claim: The majority of online detections inside reference bursts (73.8%) occurred when the rat was immobile (speed < 5 cm/s).
source: Indeed, 80.6% of FPnon_burst in RUN2 occurred when the rat was moving (speed > 5 cm/s), whereas the majority of online detections inside reference bursts (73.8%) occurred when the rat was immobile (speed < 5 cm/s).
evidence: This provides behavioral context for true positive detections.

claim: Reference population bursts that were identified online as replay events had higher posterior bias for one of the maze arms than bursts ignored by the closed-loop system.
source: Indeed, reference population bursts that were identified online as replay events had higher posterior bias (biasmax and biasmax score) for one of the maze arms than did reference bursts that were ignored by the closed-loop system (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by cumulative distribution comparisons shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Online detected events scored higher on metrics for linear spatial-temporal structure (line fit score, Pearson correlation and sequence score).
source: Likewise, online detected events scored higher on metrics for linear spatial-temporal structure (line fit score, Pearson correlation and sequence score; Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by cumulative distribution comparisons shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: These results are consistent with the closed-loop system preferentially detecting replay-containing reference bursts.
source: These results are consistent with the closed-loop system preferentially detecting replay-containing reference bursts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing higher replay metrics for detected events.

claim: Reference bursts with arm-biased posteriors (biasmax score >3) and trajectory structure (line fit score >0.1) were labeled as containing replay content for one of the maze arms.
source: For quantification purposes, and absent ground-truth replay labels, we labeled offline reference bursts with arm-biased posteriors (biasmax score >3) and trajectory structure (line fit score >0.1) as containing replay content for one of the maze arms (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to define reference replay events.

claim: Across the three sessions, 35.3% of reference bursts were associated with replay (1238/3506).
source: Across the three sessions, 35.3% of reference bursts were associated with replay (1238/3506; REST — 18.5%, 244/1321; RUN2 ﻿— 45.5%, 994/2185), of which 25.8% were classified as putative joint replay events that span more than one maze arm (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics of replay prevalence in the reference dataset.

claim: 25.8% of replay events were classified as putative joint replay events that span more than one maze arm.
source: Across the three sessions, 35.3% of reference bursts were associated with replay (1238/3506; REST — 18.5%, 244/1321; RUN2 ﻿— 45.5%, 994/2185), of which 25.8% were classified as putative joint replay events that span more than one maze arm (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This provides descriptive statistics with citation to prior work on joint replay.

claim: Single and joint replay events were correctly detected and classified in real-time in both REST and RUN2.
source: In both REST and RUN2, single and joint replay events were correctly detected and classified in real-time (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by example events shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The system correctly ignored bursts that did not contain consistent representations of any of the three maze arms.
source: The system also correctly ignored bursts that did not contain consistent representations of any of the three maze arms (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by example events shown in Figure 3c.

claim: False-positive detections were mainly caused by local matches to identification criteria in the 30 ms window without significant reference replay present across the whole population burst.
source: False-positive detections were mainly caused by local matches to the identification criteria in the 30 ms window without significant reference replay present across the whole population burst (see examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This provides an explanation for false positives with reference to examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: False-negative detections were mainly caused by failure of noisy MUA, sharpness and consistency signals to cross threshold values concurrently.
source: False-negative detections were mainly caused by failure of noisy MUA, sharpness and consistency signals to cross threshold values concurrently (see examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This provides an explanation for false negatives with reference to examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Occasionally, false-positive/-negative detections resulted from a mismatch between offline and online decoded position estimates.
source: Occasionally, false-positive/-negative detections were the result of a mismatch between the offline and online decoded position estimates, possibly resulting from compression of the encoding model or differences in spike detection.
evidence: This provides an explanation for some detection errors.

claim: A high fraction of reference bursts with replay content were correctly flagged online (median sensitivity 0.78, range: [0.60, 0.95]).
source: Overall, a high fraction of reference bursts with replay content were correctly flagged as such online (median sensitivity 0.78, range: [0.60, 0.95]) and a high fraction of non-replay reference bursts were correctly ignored by the online system (median specificity 0.71, range: [0.44, 0.80]) (Figure 4b, top; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity calculations shown in Figure 4b and Table 3.

claim: A high fraction of non-replay reference bursts were correctly ignored by the online system (median specificity 0.71, range: [0.44, 0.80]).
source: Overall, a high fraction of reference bursts with replay content were correctly flagged as such online (median sensitivity 0.78, range: [0.60, 0.95]) and a high fraction of non-replay reference bursts were correctly ignored by the online system (median specificity 0.71, range: [0.44, 0.80]) (Figure 4b, top; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by specificity calculations shown in Figure 4b and Table 3.

claim: The online detection favored a low number of false negatives at the expense of a higher number of false positives (median FOR 0.11, FDR 0.54).
source: The online detection favored a low number of false negatives at the expense of a higher number of false positives (median false omission rate (FOR) 0.11, false discovery rate (FDR) 0.54), in particular during REST (FOR 0.02, FDR 0.68) as compared to RUN2 (FOR 0.28, FDR 0.36) (Figure 4b, middle; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by FOR and FDR calculations shown in Figure 4b and Table 3.

claim: Informedness, markedness and Matthews correlation coefficient were well above zero, indicating good online identification of population bursts with replay content.
source: All three measures were well above zero, the performance score of a random classifier (Figure 4b bottom; Table 3), indicating good online identification of population bursts with replay content.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance metrics shown in Figure 4b and Table 3.

claim: For reference bursts correctly flagged online as events with replay, the actual replay content was classified with high accuracy (median content accuracy 0.95, range [0.83, 1.00]).
source: For the reference bursts that were correctly flagged by the online system as events with replay, the actual replay content (i.e. which of the three maze arms was represented in the replay event) was classified with high accuracy (Table 2; median content accuracy 0.95, range [0.83, 1.00]; REST 0.95, RUN2 0.95).
evidence: This claim is supported by content classification accuracy measurements in Table 2.

claim: Across all reference bursts detected online, the median closed-loop detection latency relative to offline-defined burst onset was 50.7 ms (90% CI [31.4, 116.2]).
source: Across all reference bursts that were detected online, the median closed-loop detection latency (Figure 4a; Table 2) relative to the offline-defined burst onset was 50.7 ms (90% CI [31.4, 116.2]) and the median relative detection latency, as percentage of the reference burst duration, was 59.5% (90% CI: [21.9, 89.0]) (Figure 4c,d; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements shown in Figure 4c,d and Table 2.

claim: The median relative detection latency, as percentage of reference burst duration, was 59.5% (90% CI: [21.9, 89.0]).
source: Across all reference bursts that were detected online, the median closed-loop detection latency (Figure 4a; Table 2) relative to the offline-defined burst onset was 50.7 ms (90% CI [31.4, 116.2]) and the median relative detection latency, as percentage of the reference burst duration, was 59.5% (90% CI: [21.9, 89.0]) (Figure 4c,d; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements shown in Figure 4c,d and Table 2.

claim: The latency for online detection of reference bursts containing replay content was similar (median detection latency 51.0 ms, 90% CI [30.3, 119.6]; median relative latency 53.6%, 90% CI [19.5, 87.4]).
source: The latency for online detection of reference bursts that contain replay content was similar (median detection latency 51.0 ms, 90% CI [30.3, 119.6]; median relative latency 53.6%, 90% CI [19.5, 87.4]).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements for replay-containing bursts.

claim: For long reference replay bursts (duration >100 ms), the median detection latency was 58.3 ms (90% CI [30.0, 127.2]) and median relative latency was 41.9% (90% CI [18.1, 84.7]).
source: For long reference replay bursts (duration >100 ms), the median detection latency was slightly higher at 58.3 ms (90% CI [30.0, 127.2]), but the median relative latency of 41.9% (90% CI [18.1, 84.7]) was lower (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency measurements for long bursts shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Online replay detection occurred well before burst offset time, making the system suitable for experiments requiring replay content-specific closed-loop manipulation.
source: These results demonstrate that online replay detection occurred well before burst offset time, thus making our hardware–software system suitable for experiments requiring replay content-specific closed-loop manipulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the latency measurements.

claim: Parameters for online replay content identification were chosen based on pilot experiments and offline simulations carried out beforehand.
source: In the experimental tests, the parameters for online replay content identification and classification were chosen on the basis of pilot experiments and offline simulations carried out beforehand.
evidence: This describes the methodology for parameter selection.

claim: Parameters may be tuned to meet specific requirements of an experiment.
source: However, such parameters may be tuned to meet the specific requirements of an experiment.
evidence: This is a statement about the flexibility of the system.

claim: In RUN2 epochs, the maximum attainable correlations were only marginally and not significantly higher than those obtained in live tests.
source: On the other hand, in the RUN2 epochs, the maximum attainable correlations were only marginally and not significantly higher than those obtained in the live tests (Table 4; Figure 5a, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of live and optimal parameters shown in Figure 5 and Table 4.

claim: Content accuracy is mainly dependent on online decoding performance and is influenced by compression threshold and number of recorded neurons.
source: Content accuracy is mainly dependent on the online decoding performance and is influenced by compression threshold (see Figure 1d) and the number of recorded neurons (or proxies thereof, such as the number of tetrodes).
evidence: This is an interpretation of factors affecting content accuracy.

claim: Detection latency is mainly dependent on the size of the integration window used to determine replay content.
source: Detection latency is mainly dependent on the size of the integration window used to determine replay content, which was fixed to 30 ms (three 10 ms bins) in the live tests.
evidence: This is an interpretation of factors affecting detection latency.

claim: Detection latency varied with the size of the integration window.
source: The simulations show that detection latency varied with the size of the integration window (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Use of smaller bin size and/or lower number of bins decreases relative detection latency at the expense of reduced detection accuracy.
source: As expected, the use of smaller bin size and/or a lower number of Nbins decreases relative detection latency, at the expense of reduced detection accuracy (i.e. lower Matthews correlation coefficient).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trade-off shown in simulations.

claim: Accurate real-time replay detection requires replay content to be predictable from the initial portion of the bursting event.
source: Accurate real-time replay detection requires replay content to be predictable from the initial portion of the bursting event.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for early detection.

claim: Higher signal-to-noise and neatly structured decoded replay trajectories are easier to detect online as they are less susceptible to short timescale signal variability.
source: Therefore, higher signal-to-noise and neatly structured decoded replay trajectories are easier to detect online as they are less susceptible to short timescale signal variability.
evidence: This is a logical inference about factors affecting detection.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio of replay is strongly influenced by the level of sampling of the spiking neuronal population.
source: Since the signal-to-noise ratio of replay is strongly influenced by the level of sampling of the spiking neuronal population (although biological factors might play a role too [Roumis and Frank, 2015; Tang et al., 2017]), spiking data recorded from poorly sampled neuronal populations are likely to lead to an increase in online replay detection errors.
evidence: This is a statement about factors affecting signal quality, supported by citations.

claim: Spiking data from poorly sampled neuronal populations are likely to lead to an increase in online replay detection errors.
source: Since the signal-to-noise ratio of replay is strongly influenced by the level of sampling of the spiking neuronal population (although biological factors might play a role too [Roumis and Frank, 2015; Tang et al., 2017]), spiking data recorded from poorly sampled neuronal populations are likely to lead to an increase in online replay detection errors.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the relationship between sampling and signal quality.

claim: Higher tetrode number decreased the variability of the MUA rate estimate within 10 ms bins.
source: Consistent with a higher signal-to-noise ratio, a higher tetrode number decreased the variability of the MUA rate estimate within 10 ms bins and increased the separability of the MUA rate distributions for non-burst periods, bursts without replay and bursts with replay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: Higher tetrode number increased the separability of MUA rate distributions for non-burst periods, bursts without replay and bursts with replay.
source: Consistent with a higher signal-to-noise ratio, a higher tetrode number decreased the variability of the MUA rate estimate within 10 ms bins and increased the separability of the MUA rate distributions for non-burst periods, bursts without replay and bursts with replay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: The sharpness of posterior probability distributions increased with higher tetrode numbers.
source: The sharpness of the posterior probability distributions increased with higher tetrode numbers, whereas the sharpness distributions for non-burst periods and bursts with replay showed a clear separation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,d.

claim: Replay identification and classification performance improved when more tetrodes were included, as evidenced by higher correlation and content accuracy measures.
source: As expected, replay identification and classification performance improved when more tetrodes were included, as evidenced by higher correlation and content accuracy measures (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Matthews correlation coefficient does not appear to saturate at the maximum number of tetrodes (14) in the test dataset.
source: Matthews correlation coefficient does not appear to saturate at the maximum number of tetrodes in the test dataset (14), suggesting that further improvement is possible by increasing the number of sampled cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trend in correlation with tetrode number.

claim: Further improvement in detection is possible by increasing the number of sampled cells.
source: Matthews correlation coefficient does not appear to saturate at the maximum number of tetrodes in the test dataset (14), suggesting that further improvement is possible by increasing the number of sampled cells.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the non-saturating trend in performance.

claim: Matthews correlation shows little variation for low number of tetrodes and improves most strongly from 10 tetrodes and up.
source: Interestingly, Matthews correlation shows little variation for low number of tetrodes and improves most strongly from 10 tetrodes and up.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of performance versus tetrode number.

claim: There is a critical subset of tetrodes that provide most of the information for accurate determination of replay content.
source: It is conceivable that, given heterogeneity in spiking data across tetrodes, there is a critical subset of tetrodes that provide most of the information for accurate determination of replay content.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the non-linear relationship between tetrode number and performance.

claim: Run-decoding performance improved with increasing number of tetrodes, as in-arm decoding error decreased and fraction of arm-correct position estimates increased.
source: As expected, cross-validated run decoding improved with increasing number of tetrodes, as in-arm decoding error decreased and the fraction of arm-correct position estimates increased (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Run-decoding performance improved rapidly up to four tetrodes and more gradually for higher tetrode counts.
source: Run-decoding performance improved rapidly up to four tetrodes and more gradually for higher tetrode counts.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of run decoding performance.

claim: Replay detection performance and run decoding performance show a low and highly non-linear correlation.
source: As a result, replay detection performance and run decoding performance show a low and highly non-linear correlation (Figure 6c), which suggests that a low run-decoding error (e.g. median error below 10 cm) is a necessary although not sufficient condition for accurate online replay detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: A low run-decoding error is a necessary although not sufficient condition for accurate online replay detection.
source: As a result, replay detection performance and run decoding performance show a low and highly non-linear correlation (Figure 6c), which suggests that a low run-decoding error (e.g. median error below 10 cm) is a necessary although not sufficient condition for accurate online replay detection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between run decoding and replay detection performance.

claim: The solution provides rapid closed-loop feedback specifically triggered by replay of experimenter-defined content.
source: Our solution provides rapid closed-loop feedback that is specifically triggered by replay of an experimenter-defined content, such as replay of a trajectory through one segment of a maze explored by the animal.
evidence: This summarizes the capability of the system.

claim: This technical advance makes it possible to perform replay content-specific perturbations to address the causal link between specific replay events and memory consolidation/retrieval processes.
source: This technical advance makes it possible to perform replay content-specific perturbations to address directly the causal link between specific replay events and memory consolidation/retrieval processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the technology.

claim: The system goes beyond recent efforts to decode or respond to hippocampal activity online.
source: Our system goes beyond recent efforts to decode or respond to hippocampal activity online.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the novelty of the work.

claim: Previous work described systems that provide real-time feedback stimulation in response to spiking activity.
source: Previous work described systems that provide real-time feedback stimulation in response to spiking activity (Nguyen et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This references prior work in the field with citations.

claim: Prior systems perform online decoding of a rat's physical location from a limited number of hippocampal place cells.
source: These systems perform online decoding of a rat's physical location from a limited number of hippocampal place cells (Guger et al., 2011)
evidence: This references prior work with citation.

claim: Prior systems implement online spike-sorting with simultaneous detection of ripple oscillations.
source: or implement online spike-sorting with simultaneous detection of ripple oscillations (Sethi and Kemere, 2015).
evidence: This references prior work with citation.

claim: None of the prior studies addressed the combination of short timescale neural decoding and low-latency detection of replayed spike sequences.
source: However, none of these prior studies addressed the combination of short timescale neural decoding and low-latency detection of replayed spike sequences.
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior work that the current study addresses.

claim: de Lavilléon et al. (2015) showed that coupling spikes of a single hippocampal place cell during rest to electrical stimulation induced a subsequent preference for the cell's place field.
source: de Lavilléon et al. (2015) showed that coupling spikes of a single hippocampal place cell during rest to electrical stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle induced a subsequent preference of the animal for the cell's place field.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited prior study.

claim: In de Lavilléon et al. (2015), the association with replay was only speculative as no multi-neuronal pattern was being detected.
source: Still, the association with replay was only speculative as no multi-neuronal pattern was being detected.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of limitations in prior work.

claim: Deng et al. (2016) developed an algorithm for rapid hippocampal replay content classification in the awake state using state-space models.
source: Finally, Deng et al. (2016) developed an algorithm for rapid hippocampal replay content classification in the awake state using state-space models.
evidence: This summarizes a cited prior study.

claim: Despite low algorithmic latency in Deng et al. (2016), the computational latency was prohibitive and the algorithm's application to live data streams was neither demonstrated nor fully conceptualized.
source: Despite the low algorithmic latency and the solid mathematical framework of their strategy, the computational latency was still prohibitive and the algorithm's application to live data streams in an experiment was neither demonstrated nor fully conceptualized.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of limitations in prior work.

claim: The replay detection technology has similarities with brain-computer interfaces and neuroprosthetics research.
source: Our replay detection technology has similarities and differences with the large body of research in brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) and neuroprosthetics (Lebedev and Nicolelis, 2006).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the relationship to other fields.

claim: In common with some invasive BCIs, online population decoding was applied to unsorted large-scale single-unit recordings.
source: In common with some prototypes of invasive BCIs used for controlling external devices (Fraser et al., 2009; Li and Li, 2017), we applied online population decoding to unsorted large-scale single-unit recordings.
evidence: This identifies a similarity with prior BCI work, supported by citations.

claim: The use of high-level signals relating to cognitive processes rather than pure motor function is not new in neuroprosthetics.
source: The use of high-level signals that relate to cognitive processes such action planning or memory rather than to pure motor function is not new in neuroprosthetics (see cognitive neural prosthetics (Andersen et al., 2010; Hampson et al., 2018).
evidence: This references prior work in cognitive neuroprosthetics with citations.

claim: The development of a 'replay BCI' faced the unique challenge that the content of hippocampal replay does not have a 'ground truth'.
source: In contrast to other BCI and neuroprosthetics applications, the development of a 'replay BCI' faced two unique challenges. First, while it is possible to test the accuracy of BCIs by measuring the difference between desired and actual output, the content of hippocampal replay does not have a 'ground truth' and requires assumptions and statistical analyses to quantify the goodness of the output.
evidence: This identifies a unique challenge in the current work compared to other BCIs.

claim: The most difficult challenge relates to the strict latency specifications in generating online feedback.
source: The second and most difficult challenge relates to the strict latency specifications in generating an online feedback.
evidence: This identifies the primary technical challenge addressed by the work.

claim: BCIs can operate with processing latency of less than 50 ms when using slowly sampled EEG signals on few channels.
source: BCIs can operate with a processing latency of less than 50 ms when using slowly sampled (below 4800 Hz) EEG signals on few (8–32) channels (Fischer et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2010).
evidence: This references performance characteristics of prior BCIs with citations.

claim: BCIs using rapidly sampled signals for spike detection on larger electrode arrays can reach latencies as low as 120 ms.
source: BCIs using rapidly sampled signals for spike detection on larger electrode arrays can reach latencies as low as 120 ms (Velliste et al., 2008)
evidence: This references performance characteristics of prior BCIs with citation.

claim: Lower latencies than 120 ms are not necessary for motor BCIs as natural control of motor output has a natural delay of 150-200 ms.
source: lower latencies are however not necessary as the natural control of motor output has a natural delay of 150 – 200 ms (Velliste et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This explains why lower latencies are not required for motor BCIs, supported by citations.

claim: The current system surpassed prior BCI limits by using more than 50 channels sampled at 32 kHz to generate brain state estimates every 10 ms and classify replay patterns with ~50 ms average latency.
source: Here, we surpassed these limits by using more than 50 channels sampled at 32 kHz to generate estimates of brain state (animals' position) every 10 ms and to classify hippocampal replay patterns with ~50 ms average latency.
evidence: This is a comparative statement highlighting the achievement of the current work.

claim: A trade-off was made between the earliest possible prediction of replay content and the most accurate possible prediction.
source: As with any system that aims to provide on-time feedback, a trade-off was made between the earliest possible prediction of replay content in a population burst and the most accurate possible prediction.
evidence: This describes a fundamental design consideration.

claim: The trade-off is reflected in the numbers of incorrect detections and omissions when compared to a reference replay content classification.
source: This trade-off is reflected in the numbers of incorrect detections and omissions, when compared to a reference replay content classification.
evidence: This describes how the trade-off manifests in performance metrics.

claim: The experimental goals determine how the best trade-off is made.
source: Ultimately, the experimental goals determine how the best trade-off is made.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental design considerations.

claim: For a balanced trade-off between true and false positives/negatives, the Matthews correlation coefficient was chosen as a measure of performance.
source: For a balanced trade-off between true and false positives/negatives, we opted for the Matthews correlation coefficient as a measure of performance.
evidence: This describes the choice of performance metric.

claim: Similar datasets collected beforehand are a guide to actual parameter selection.
source: While the exact parameter values depend on the data and optimal values are not known prior to the experiment, similar datasets collected beforehand (without disruptive closed-loop manipulations) are a guide to the actual parameter selection.
evidence: This provides practical guidance for using the system.

claim: The latency-accuracy trade-off is affected by the performance of neural decoding.
source: The trade-off between accuracy and latency is affected by the performance of neural decoding.
evidence: This identifies a factor affecting the trade-off.

claim: A high cell yield in recordings will improve decoding performance and is expected to lead to better online replay detection.
source: A high cell yield in the recordings will improve decoding performance and hence is expected to lead to better online replay detection.
evidence: This is a prediction about factors that will improve performance.

claim: The no-spike-sort decoding approach helps by utilizing information from all available spikes.
source: The no-spike-sort decoding approach (Kloosterman et al., 2014), which is at the core of our solution, helps by utilizing the information from all available spikes, whether or not they are part of well-isolated cell clusters.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the decoding approach with citation to prior work.

claim: Compression of the encoding model and software parallelization provided the necessary computational speed-up.
source: Compression of the encoding model and software parallelization in Falcon provided the necessary computational speed-up, which in our system results in the availability of the animal's replayed position within 2 ms of data arrival, with acceptable decoding accuracy loss.
evidence: This describes technical approaches that enabled fast computation.

claim: A shorter window of integration results in lower detection latencies and increased focus on local, noisy features.
source: A second factor that contributes to the latency-accuracy trade-off is the amount of recent data considered for classifying replay content online. In the content classification algorithm, a shorter window of integration (i.e. fewer bins and/or smaller bin sizes) results in lower detection latencies, and also in an increased focus on local, noisy features of the data that may not be consistent with replay content across the complete event.
evidence: This describes another factor affecting the latency-accuracy trade-off.

claim: A window of 30 ms resulted in good replay content detection within short latencies.
source: We settled on a window of 30 ms, which resulted in good replay content detection within short latencies.
evidence: This describes the choice of integration window and its outcome.

claim: Further decrease of false-positive and negative detection could be achieved by an extension that adaptively increases the time window to accumulate additional evidence.
source: In future work, further decrease of false-positive and negative detection could be achieved by an extension of our algorithm that adaptively increases the time window to accumulate additional evidence until a certain level of confidence that the event under consideration does or does not represent the target replay content has been reached.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement.

claim: Further improvement of online replay detection is possible by increasing the sampling of spiking data.
source: Further improvement of online replay detection is possible by increasing the sampling of spiking data (e.g. by increasing number of recording channels), as the performance in our tests with up to 14 tetrodes did not yet reach a plateau.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the non-saturating performance with tetrode number.

claim: Increased spiking data will improve both the MUA burst detection and replay content determination components of the online algorithm.
source: The increased spiking data will improve both the MUA burst detection and replay content determination components of the online algorithm.
evidence: This is a prediction about how increased data will improve performance.

claim: Increased data may allow further reduction of the integration window, as this is the main determinant of detection latency.
source: This may also allow a further reduction of the integration window, as this is the main determinant of the detection latency.
evidence: This is a prediction about potential improvements.

claim: The system will be able to handle additional computational burden without significantly increasing computational latency.
source: The system as presented will be able to handle the additional computational burden without increasing the computational latency significantly, as it scales to at least 128 recording channels (32 tetrodes) and probably more when run on a 32-core workstation.
evidence: This is a statement about the scalability of the system based on stress tests.

claim: Scaling to several hundreds or thousands of recording channels may require offloading computationally intensive neural decoding steps to the GPU.
source: Scaling to several hundreds or thousands of recording channels in future implementations may require offloading the computationally intensive neural decoding steps to the graphics processing unit (GPU).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future scaling of the system.

claim: Ground truth replay labels are unavailable for hippocampal replay events.
source: The detection of hippocampal replay events has to take into account that ground truth replay labels are unavailable.
evidence: This is a statement about a fundamental limitation in evaluating replay detection.

claim: Detected events score higher on measures that correlate with replay content.
source: To evaluate the performance of online replay detection, we showed that detected events score higher on measures that correlate with replay content and that detections largely agree with an offline-defined reference.
evidence: This describes the approach used to validate online detection performance.

claim: The quality of the offline reference depends on the parameters of the offline detector and on sufficient sampling of spiking data.
source: The quality of the offline reference – that is, how well it captures the desired target replay content – depends on the parameters of the offline detector and on sufficient sampling of spiking data.
evidence: This identifies factors affecting the quality of the reference dataset.

claim: The offline detector has the advantage of access to all data and not being bound by limited compute time.
source: The offline detector has the advantage of access to all data and of not being bound by limited compute time, whereas the the online detector includes compromises to perform fast and early real-time detection.
evidence: This describes a fundamental difference between offline and online detection.

claim: One would generally have higher confidence in the offline reference and would tune parameters of the online detector using prior knowledge or training data.
source: Hence, one would generally have a higher confidence in the offline reference and would accordingly tune the parameters of the online detector using either prior knowledge or training data.
evidence: This provides guidance on how to use the system.

claim: Reliance on an inappropriate reference without careful verification will make experiments manipulating online detected replay events difficult to interpret.
source: Still, depending on parameters, the offline reference may vary from being too inclusive (e.g. all population bursts are marked as replay) to overly exclusive (e.g. no population bursts are marked as replay) and reliance on an inappropriate reference without careful verification will make experiments that manipulate online detected replay events difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about the importance of proper reference definition.

claim: Run decoding was less sensitive to data degradation than replay detection.
source: Another cautionary note should be made about using decoding performance during run to predict subsequent online replay detection performance: in our tests, run decoding was less sensitive to data degradation and although low run decoding error may be required for good decoding of replay content, it is not a sufficient condition.
evidence: This is a cautionary note based on the analysis of run decoding versus replay detection.

claim: Detection latency of online replay detection was on average ~50 ms.
source: Detection latency of online replay detection was on average ~50 ms.
evidence: This summarizes a key performance metric.

claim: Previous work demonstrated online burst detection (without replay content identification) at ~40 ms latency.
source: In our previous work, using the same hardware–software system, we demonstrated online burst detection (without replay content identification) at ~40 ms latency (Ciliberti and Kloosterman, 2017).
evidence: This references prior work by the authors with citation.

claim: By combining burst and replay content detection, on average only 10 ms was added to the time needed for basic population burst detection.
source: Here, by combining burst and replay content detection in the algorithm, on average we added only 10 ms to the time that is needed for a basic population burst detection in the same closed-loop system.
evidence: This is a comparison showing the modest additional latency for content detection.

claim: The rate of false-positive detections outside candidate replay population bursts were generally low in rest but more prevalent during active maze exploration.
source: The rate of false-positive detections outside candidate replay population bursts were generally low in rest, but more prevalent when the rat was actively exploring the maze, probably due to a higher mean population firing rate during motion than during rest.
evidence: This describes a pattern in false positive detections with a speculative explanation.

claim: Information about the animal's behavior or replay-associated electrophysiological markers are often used in offline analyses to reduce false positives.
source: In offline analyses, information about the animal's behavior (e.g. running speed) or replay-associated electrophysiological markers (e.g. high-frequency ripple oscillation power) are often used to reduce this category of false positives (Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This references a common practice in offline analysis with citation.

claim: Integration of additional information in a Falcon processing pipeline would be straightforward but may increase detection latency and introduce new sources of errors.
source: The integration of this additional information in a Falcon processing pipeline would be relative straightforward, but this strategy may increase detection latency and introduce new sources of errors.
evidence: This discusses potential modifications to the system with consideration of trade-offs.

claim: Incorporation of the real-time replay detection solution in an experiment requires that an encoding model is built from spiking data recorded during initial maze exploration.
source: The incorporation of our real-time replay detection solution in an experiment requires that an encoding model is built from spiking data recorded during an initial exploration of the maze.
evidence: This describes a requirement for using the system.

claim: At present, the encoding model is constructed manually offline and uploaded during a brief pause between initial maze exploration and start of real-time replay detection.
source: At present, the encoding model is constructed manually offline and uploaded into the Falcon software during a brief pause of 5 – 15 min between the end of the initial maze exploration and the start of the real-time replay detection.
evidence: This describes the current workflow for using the system.

claim: Future enhancements will enable construction and validation of the encoding model online rather than offline.
source: Future enhancements will enable the construction and validation of the encoding model online rather than offline: besides reducing experimental down-time, this will provide immediate feedback on the decoding performance and will enable content-specific closed-loop manipulation of awake replay events as soon as the quality of the encoding model is sufficient.
evidence: This describes planned future improvements to the system.

claim: The target replay content for online detection was the representation of one of three maze arms.
source: In our demonstration, the target replay content for online detection was the representation of one of three maze arms.
evidence: This describes the specific target used in the demonstration.

claim: The system can be trivially extended to environments composed of more than three arms and to target joint replay content covering multiple maze arms in succession.
source: The system can be trivially extended to environments that are composed of more than three arms (e.g. 8-arm radial mazes or set of linear tracks) and to target joint replay content that covers multiple maze arms in succession.
evidence: This describes potential extensions of the system.

claim: A local spatial derivative criterion may be added for more strict detection of replay trajectories.
source: For more strict detection of replay trajectories, a local spatial derivative criterion may be added to the replay classification algorithm.
evidence: This suggests a potential enhancement to the algorithm.

claim: Extension of the encoding model with running direction would form the basis of a detector for forward and reverse replay events.
source: Together with an extension of the encoding model with running direction (Davidson et al., 2009), such a trajectory criterion would form the basis of a detector for forward and reverse replay events (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This suggests a potential enhancement with citations to prior work on forward/reverse replay.

claim: By altering the encoding model, the system could be used to target other types of replay content.
source: By altering the encoding model, the system could also be used to target other types of replay content, including reactivation of immobility-associated place cells (Yu et al., 2017), non-spatial task-related replay (Takahashi, 2015), sequence reactivation of time cells (Pastalkova et al., 2008) or spiking sequences in nested theta/gamma oscillations during active behavior (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes potential applications with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: The approach is not limited to hippocampal replay bursts and could be applied to cortical or subcortical replay.
source: Our approach is not limited to hippocampal replay bursts and could be applied to cortical (Ji and Wilson, 2007; Peyrache et al., 2009) or subcortical (Lansink et al., 2009) replay as long as it is possible to define a decodable and detectable content.
evidence: This describes the generalizability of the approach with citations to replay in other brain regions.

claim: The approach presented will pave the way for a new generation of closed-loop experiments aimed at elucidating the causal role of internally generated neural activity in memory processes and cognition.
source: The approach presented here will pave the way for a new generation of closed-loop experiments aimed at elucidating the causal role of hippocampal and non-hippocampal internally generated neural activity in memory processes and cognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the technology.
